content.text:
## QC run

Ran **FastQC v0.13.0** on `/fixtures/reads_R1.fastq.gz` and `/fixtures/reads_R2.fastq.gz`, then verified the flagged modules directly against the raw reads in Python and spot-checked read origin with NCBI BLAST (`blastn`/`core_nt`).

### FastQC module status

| Module | R1 | R2 |
|---|---|---|
| Basic Statistics | PASS | PASS |
| Per base sequence quality | PASS | PASS |
| Per sequence quality scores | PASS | PASS |
| Per base sequence content | PASS | PASS |
| **Per sequence GC content** | **FAIL** | **FAIL** |
| Per base N content | PASS | PASS |
| Sequence Length Distribution | PASS | PASS |
| Sequence Duplication Levels | PASS | PASS |
| Overrepresented sequences | WARN | WARN |
| Adapter Content | PASS | PASS |

### Basic stats (FastQC)
- 4,000 reads per file, 100 bp fixed length, 400 kbp per file; encoding Sanger/Illumina 1.9; %GC 53
- Pairing verified in Python: read IDs identical and in identical order in both files, 1:1, no duplicate IDs
- 0 N bases in either file (0.0000%)
- 0.0% adapter at every position for all FastQC adapter sets (one trivial exception: PolyA peaks at 0.51% in R2)
- Duplication: 87.1% (R1) / 87.4% (R2) deduplicated → ~13% duplicates

### The two findings that matter

**1. The quality scores are not real.** Every base in every read is exactly Q40 — the quality string is the character `I` repeated, 400,000/400,000 bases in each file, zero variance. FastQC itself tripped on this ("Using Phred32 encoding your lowest quality is 41, could this file be Phred64 encoded?"). Real Illumina data always shows a 3'-end quality decay and a spread of per-read means. These are simulated/synthetic reads. The `Per base sequence quality` PASS is therefore vacuous, and anything that models base quality (BQSR, variant-caller quality priors) will behave unrealistically on them.

**2. The GC FAIL is compositional, not contamination.** The distribution is bimodal, computed directly from R1:
- 1,657 reads (41.4%) at mean GC 37.5%
- 2,343 reads (58.6%) at mean GC 64.5%
- overall mean 53.4%; mates fall in the same GC mode 84.3% of the time

I BLASTed representative reads from both modes. All hits were human at 100% identity / 100% coverage, E = 8.5e-43:
- high-GC → `AL627309` (human chr1 clone RP11-34P13) and `Z95704` (human 4PTEL, chr4p16.3)
- low-GC → `AC104056` (human cosmid from chr2)

Both high-GC hits are **subtelomeric**, and the telomeric hexamer `(CCCTAA)x2` appears in 5.7% of R1 reads — elevated for a whole-genome library. The overrepresented-sequence WARN is driven by the same thing (telomeric `CCCTAACCCTAA...` and GC-rich repeats, each only 0.13% of reads). So the GC-rich mode is human subtelomere/GC-rich sequence, not a foreign organism. Caveat: this is a 3-read spot check, not an exhaustive contamination screen — I did not run a full taxonomic classifier (none is available here).

**Also worth knowing:** read IDs are monotonic but run `read00001` … `read14637` with only 4,000 present. These files are a pre-filtered or subsampled ~27% subset of a larger read set, not a complete run.

### Usability
There is nothing to clean up — no adapter contamination, no N's, no quality trimming needed, properly synchronized pairs, acceptable duplication. But the data is only 800 kbp total across both mates, i.e. ~0.0003× coverage of a human genome, and the quality scores are synthetic. It is fine as pipeline test/validation input and useless as a biological dataset. If you expected this to be a real sequencing run, something is wrong upstream in how the file was generated or handed to you.

## ANSWER

**Usable as test data only — not as a real dataset.**

- FastQC v0.13.0: 8/10 modules PASS both mates; `Per sequence GC content` **FAIL**, `Overrepresented sequences` **WARN**.
- 4,000 reads/file, 100 bp, correctly paired, 0 N's, 0% adapter, ~13% duplicates.
- **Quality scores are synthetic**: all 400,000 bases per file are exactly Q40, zero variance → simulated reads, not a real run.
- **GC FAIL is bimodal** (41.4% of reads at GC 37.5%, 58.6% at GC 64.5%), caused by human subtelomeric/GC-rich sequence, not contamination — BLAST hits `AL627309`, `Z95704` (4PTEL), `AC104056`, all human at 100% identity/coverage, E=8.5e-43.
- Too small for any genome-scale analysis (~0.0003× human coverage) and is a ~27% subset of a larger read set (IDs 1–14,637).
- No trimming or filtering would improve them; the limitation is the data itself.
